name: Thalamoperforating and thalamogeniculate arteries
summary: Small perforating branches from the P1 segment of the posterior cerebral artery and the posterior communicating artery supply the thalamus. The paramedian (posterior thalamoperforating) group from P1 feeds the medial thalamus and rostral midbrain; when a single trunk from one P1 supplies both sides (artery of Percheron), its occlusion causes bilateral paramedian thalamic infarcts with coma-like somnolence and vertical gaze palsy. The thalamogeniculate arteries from P2 supply the lateral thalamus and are the usual cause of the pure sensory stroke and thalamic pain syndrome.

anatomy.location: Arise from the posterior aspect of the P1 segments in the interpeduncular fossa and from the posterior communicating artery (anterior thalamoperforators), entering the posterior perforated substance beside the mammillary bodies; the thalamogeniculates leave the P2 segment in the ambient cistern and enter the thalamus beneath the geniculate bodies.

subdivisions.name: Anterior (tuberothalamic) group
subdivisions.note: from PComm: anterior nuclei, mammillothalamic tract; amnesia and apathy when infarcted

subdivisions.name: Paramedian (posterior thalamoperforating) group
subdivisions.note: from P1: mediodorsal nucleus, intralaminar nuclei, rostral midbrain; artery of Percheron variant

subdivisions.name: Inferolateral (thalamogeniculate) group
subdivisions.note: from P2: ventral posterior nuclei, ventral lateral nucleus; pure sensory stroke

subdivisions.name: Posterior choroidal group
subdivisions.note: pulvinar, lateral geniculate body, medial thalamus

function: Supply the thalamic relay and association nuclei and the paramedian midbrain, including the oculomotor nuclear complex and the reticular activating system at the mesodiencephalic junction.

bestView.label: interpeduncular fossa where the paramedian perforators enter
medial and lateral thalamus, the infarct sites
paramedian thalamus on both sides of the third ventricle

imaging.normalAppearance: Not visible on routine MRI; the territories are the medial thalamus flanking the third ventricle (paramedian) and the lateral thalamus beside the posterior limb of the capsule (inferolateral).

pathology.finding: Symmetrical restricted diffusion in the paramedian thalami, often with a V-shaped lesion in the rostral midbrain along the interpeduncular fossa; CT is frequently normal early.
pathology.pitfalls: Bilateral thalamic swelling on FLAIR can mimic deep venous thrombosis or a glioma; check DWI and the internal cerebral veins

pathology.finding: A small diffusion-restricting lesion in the ventral posterolateral thalamus producing a contralateral pure hemisensory syndrome.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: DWI with thin slices through the thalamus; MRV if bilateral thalamic edema without restriction

lesionEffects.deficit: Hypersomnolence or coma with vertical gaze palsy
lesionEffects.mechanism: Bilateral paramedian thalamic and rostral midbrain infarction (artery of Percheron)
Anterior and mediodorsal nuclei and the mammillothalamic tract

lesionEffects.deficit: Pure hemisensory loss, later central pain

examination: Test vertical saccades and pursuit and look for skew deviation
Bedside memory and attention testing once alert
Pin-prick, temperature and vibration over the face, arm and leg
pearls: Sudden coma with bilateral thalamic infarcts and no other explanation should prompt a search for a basilar tip embolus
All modalities lost on one side of the body including the face, with no weakness, is a thalamic lesion
